newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia drug baron agrees to pay $105 million fine.
newsitem.headline: Colombia drug baron agrees to pay $105 million fine.

text.p: Gilberto Rodriguez Orejuela, the jailed kingpin of Colombia's Cali drug cartel, agreed to pay a $105 million fine on Tuesday in a plea-bargain deal that could lead to his early release, judicial officials said.
They said the fine would be the biggest ever paid in Colombia's turbulent legal history.

Rodriguez, a reputed billionaire and the heavyweight of Colombia's crime world, agreed to pay the fine on confessing to the drug-related charge of illicit enrichment in day-long testimony to a "faceless" or anonymous judge.
A spokesman for chief prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso said Rodriguez also confessed to 19 counts of fraud stemming from his use of bank accounts to handle the illicit proceeds of his drug empire.
He also confessed to using some of those accounts to finance electoral campaigns in Colombia, the spokesman said.

The Cali cartel -- which U.S. officials have described as the world's largest drug trafficking organisation -- has been accused of providing about $6 million in contributions to the 1994 campaign of President Ernesto Samper.
Valdivieso's spokesman declined to comment on whether Rodriguez shed any new light on the scandal dogging Samper, but he described it as a major breakthrough.
"He has admitted to managing accounts for financial campaigns...for a series of political campaigns that he opened accounts for," he said. "It's the first time he's done this."

The Colombian Congress cleared Samper of any wrongdoing in relation to his campaign finances earlier this year in a trial that was dismissed as a whitewash by many critics, including U.S. diplomats. The case could, however, be reopened based on new evidence uncovered by Valdivieso.
Gilberto Rodriguez and his younger brother Miguel were jailed during a crackdown on their cartel that U.S. experts say once controlled 80 percent of the world's cocaine trade.
Both have confessed to drug-related crimes but neither has been sentenced so far.

Gilberto, the cartel's mastermind known by his nickname as "the chess player," faced a maximum of 18 years in prison with time off for cooperating with the authorities and confessing to some of his crimes, Valdivieso's spokesman said.
Additional time could be shaved off his sentence for good behaviour and academic studies undertaken while serving time in the maximum security wing of Bogota's La Picota jail.
